summary: Describes a methodology for benchmarking MPLS Fast Reroute link and node protection. It gives test setups and procedures for measuring failover times, taking into account factors that affect recovery for real-time traffic. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way to time how fast traffic switches to a backup road when the main road is blocked, so you can compare different systems fairly.

subtitle: A standard way to test and measure recovery time when network links fail.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to evaluate and compare how quickly MPLS Fast Reroute protection mechanisms recover from link and node failures. Without a standard methodology, test results are inconsistent and incomparable.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a comprehensive benchmarking methodology including reference topologies, failure scenarios, test procedures, and measurement methods. It focuses on data-plane failover using packet loss metrics.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can now objectively measure failover performance across different network equipment and compare vendors fairly.

today: RFC 6894 is an Informational document published in March 2013 that remains in use as the standard benchmarking methodology for MPLS Fast Reroute. It is referenced in network equipment specifications and used by service providers to validate and compare failover performance.

sections.title: Fast Reroute Protection
sections.content:
Modern networks use MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) to create traffic engineered tunnels that carry data along specific paths. Fast Reroute (FRR) is a protection mechanism that detects when a link or node fails and automatically switches traffic to a backup path within milliseconds. This minimizes service disruption and keeps real-time applications (like VoIP and video) working through failures.

Different network devices implement Fast Reroute differently. A device from Vendor A might recover in 50 milliseconds; a device from Vendor B might recover in 200 milliseconds. Service providers need a standard way to measure this recovery time so they can choose equipment intelligently and understand the actual service quality they are providing.

This document provides that standard methodology. It specifies how to set up test networks, introduce failures, measure recovery, and report results in a consistent way.
sections.eli5: When traffic on a network takes a detour around a broken link, you want to know how long that detour takes. Different network devices handle detours differently, so you need a fair way to measure and compare them.

sections.title: What This Methodology Covers
sections.content:
This methodology focuses on facility backup Fast Reroute, where a backup tunnel is pre-established to protect a specific link or node. The tests measure the time between a failure event and the moment traffic successfully switches to the backup path and recovers.

The tests cover both link protection (protecting a single link) and node protection (protecting an entire node). The methodology applies to various network scenarios including IP-based traffic, Layer 3 VPN services, and Layer 2 Virtual Circuits. It uses the data plane (actual user traffic) to measure failover, not control plane signaling alone.

Out of scope: testing based on specific failure detection methods like BFD, correlated failures from shared resources, control plane performance, and reoptimization of paths after failover. The tests cover facility backup only, not IP Fast Reroute or MPLS Transport Profile variants.
sections.eli5: This explains how to test the main types of backup routes: protecting a single link, or protecting an entire router. It uses real traffic to measure how fast the switch happens, not internal signaling messages.

sections.title: Test Setup and Reference Topologies
sections.content:
Tests use a reference topology with routers R1 through R6, a traffic generator, and a traffic analyzer. The device being tested (the Device Under Test or DUT) acts as the Point of Local Repair (PLR)—the router that detects the failure and switches to the backup path. Testing can position the PLR as a head-end router (starting the tunnel) or as a midpoint router (in the middle of the tunnel).

The document provides eight detailed topologies covering combinations of link and node protection with different primary and backup path lengths (from 1 to 3+ hops). Each topology accounts for how the label stack changes during failover. The methodology records the number of lost packets, out-of-order packets, and duplicate packets generated during the failure and recovery process. It also measures additive latency (delay introduced during recovery) and reversion time (time to switch back to the primary path).
sections.eli5: The test sets up routers in different patterns: some protect a single link, some protect an entire router. Each pattern tests how fast and clean the switchover is, counting broken packets and measuring delay.

sections.title: Measurement Methods and Reporting
sections.content:
The document defines three methods for calculating failover time from measured packet loss:

Packet-Loss-Based Method: Counts lost packets and divides by the traffic rate. Simple but less precise. Time-Based Loss Method: Records the time interval between the last successful packet and the first successful packet after recovery. Requires test equipment with millisecond-precision timing. Timestamp-Based Method: Embeds timestamps in each packet payload, allowing detection of out-of-order and duplicate packets, not just loss. Most accurate and recommended.

Tests MUST be performed at multiple traffic rates and with different numbers of LSP tunnels and routes protected by the PLR, since failover time may vary with scale. Test results MUST report the configuration, the number of lost/duplicate/out-of-order packets, the measured failover time in milliseconds, and details of the failure detection method used (physical alarms, RSVP hellos, or BFD). This allows fair comparison across implementations.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to measure how long the detour takes. The best way looks at the timestamp on each packet so you see exactly when traffic stopped and started again. You test with different amounts of traffic to see if it changes the recovery time.
